rows.say: A program derived address is a unique account address created deterministically from seeds and a program ID, so the same inputs always produce the same address. The bump is a small number added to the seeds to ensure the address falls off the Ed25519 curve and is a valid PDA — without it, the derived address might land on the curve and not be a valid account. A common trap is thinking the bump is random; it's actually deterministic and should be stored on the account to save compute costs if you need it again.

rows.say: A program signs for a PDA in a cross program invocation by passing the PDA's seeds and bump seed to invoke_signed() or with_signer() in a CpiContext. The runtime derives the PDA from those seeds and bump and uses it to sign the inner instruction without needing the actual private key.

rows.say: As of September 2026, a legacy or v0 transaction is capped at 1,232 bytes. The new v1 format, live since 15 September, raises that to 4,096 bytes and carries larger data over QUIC instead of UDP. A common trap: thinking the limit is 10,000 bytes — that's account data space, not transaction size.

rows.say: A single transaction can lock up to 64 accounts, or 128 if a feature flag is activated — though the hard ceiling is 256. It's a common belief that you can lock as many as you want, but the runtime enforces a strict limit to prevent one transaction from blocking others.

rows.say: As of September 2026, versioned transactions let you use Address Lookup Tables to shrink transaction size, and version 1 raises the size limit from 1,232 to 4,096 bytes. A common misconception: versioned transactions don't cost less in fees, just fit more accounts into the same transaction.

rows.say: An address lookup table stores addresses onchain, so a transaction references them by their 1-byte index instead of repeating the full 32-byte address. That shrinks the transaction. This only works in v0 transactions, which cap at 1,232 bytes; the newer v1 format dropped lookup tables for a bigger 4,096-byte limit instead.

rows.say: As of September 2026, each instruction gets a default of 200,000 compute units, and a transaction can ask for up to 1,400,000 CUs total. A common trap: if you don't explicitly set the limit early in your transaction, you'll hit the per-instruction default and fail before reaching later instructions that extend it.

rows.say: As of September 2026, rent is no longer collected from accounts, but a token account must still hold a minimum balance when created for rent exemption—about 0.00203928 SOL for a standard token account. That balance comes back when you close the account.

rows.say: As of September 2026, no rent is collected from accounts on Solana — SIMD-0084 turned collection off and the code has been removed. What remains is rent exemption: accounts must hold a minimum balance when created, but that comes back when closed. A common outdated belief is that ongoing rent payments drain balances over time.

rows.say: An associated token account is derived from your wallet address, so there's just one main account per token per person, making it easy for others to send you tokens without needing to know a custom account address. With a regular token account, you could have many of them for the same token, so senders wouldn't know which one to use.

rows.say: A mint account stores the general info about a token, like supply limits. A token account holds the actual tokens of that mint and has an owner who can transfer or burn them. Anyone can send tokens to a token account, but only the owner can send them out.

rows.say: As of September 2026, the init constraint creates a new account in the same instruction, paying for its rent exemption from a payer you name. Anchor writes an 8-byte discriminator to it, so your space parameter must include those 8 bytes. A common trap: init_if_needed looks simpler but opens a re-initialisation risk where someone pre-creates the address with malicious data.

rows.say: Anchor adds an 8-byte discriminator to the start of every account to identify its type, as the Anchor documentation explains. When you allocate space for an account, you must add 8 to your struct size in the space constraint. As of September 2026, this is still how Anchor ensures no account can be substituted for another.

rows.say: The seeds constraint verifies the PDA is derived from the correct inputs, and the bump constraint ensures it falls off the Ed25519 curve with the canonical bump—the lowest value that works, which prevents attackers substituting a different account. As of September 2026, both constraints must be used together in Anchor.

rows.say: As of September 2026, has_one checks that a field named in the constraint matches an address or public key stored inside the account data, and fails the transaction if it does not. A common trap: it does not prevent the account itself from being forged — pair it with seeds or owner to verify the account is the one you expect.

rows.say: Error 2006 means the address you passed doesn't match the PDA derived from the seeds constraint in your program. Check that instruction arguments are in the same order in your derive(Accounts) macro as in the function signature, and that you're passing the right values when calling it.

rows.say: Error 3012, AccountNotInitialized, as of September 2026 occurs when you pass an account to an instruction that expects it to be initialized but Anchor finds it empty. Common case: you're trying to init a PDA through a CPI when the parent program itself needs to initialize it—use an UncheckedAccount instead, not an initialized account type.

As of September 2026, this usually happens when you're trying to link accounts together but the address doesn't match what the program expects.

rows.say: AccountOwnedByWrongProgram (3007) means the account passed to the instruction is owned by a different program than the instruction expected: the owner field on the account doesn't match the program trying to use it. This is an Anchor account constraint error, not a scam concern.
